hypothesis: Obligate cave (troglobitic) species in North America and in Europe each have their closest surface relatives, at genus and family level, on their own continent, and the two continents' cave faunas are not more similar to each other than to their own surface faunas.
pass_criterion: Take a predefined list of at least 100 named troglobitic species, with at least 30 per continent, drawn from published cave-fauna checklists. Resolve each to genus and family in the GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Among species whose genus contains surface-dwelling congeners, at least 80% of North American cave species must have the majority of those congeners' occurrence records on the Americas, and at least 80% of European cave species must have them in Europe. Also, the share of cave genera found on both continents must be below 10%, and below the share of surface genera shared across the two continents.
fail_criterion: Fewer than 60% of cave species in either continent have a majority of their surface congeners on their own continent. Alternatively, the fraction of cave genera shared between America and Europe is 20% or more, or is higher than the fraction of surface genera shared between them.
interpretation: Darwin's 'affinities' is read as taxonomic closeness, meaning shared genus or family in the modern classification. 'Cave-animals of America' is read as obligate subterranean species (troglobites) of North America, and 'inhabitants of that continent' as surface species whose records fall in the same continent. The GBIF Backbone Taxonomy supplies the classification used to place each species in its genus and family. Continent of surface relatives would come from GBIF occurrence records of those genera, reached through the same GBIF API. The Backbone Taxonomy is the single dataset named here. This is a limitation: it records taxonomy but not geography, so the geographic step depends on GBIF occurrence data that is linked to the same names. The list of cave species is also taken from outside sources. Modern phylogenies could refine the genus and family proxy, but the test keeps to Darwin's own claim about affinities.

dataset.name: GBIF Backbone Taxonomy
dataset.why_it_fits: It is a public, open API and download resource that gives a consistent genus and family placement for every species name, including cave species. It links to GBIF occurrence records with country and continent fields. The fields used are scientificName, genus, family, rank and taxonomicStatus. The occurrence step would use countryCode and continent.
